title: Token Bucket Rate Limiter with Local In-Memory Lock Contention
subtitle: Eliminating Spinlock Degradation via Lock-Free Atomic CAS and Striped Counters
problem_statement: An in-memory rate limiter protecting an authentication endpoint under 25,000 RPS experiences severe CPU saturation. Thread profiling indicates 92% of CPU time is spent in thread parking and lock synchronization inside the TokenBucket.tryConsume() method.

faded_bug.description: Coarse synchronized method serializes all worker threads, generating massive CPU cache line invalidations.

invariants.description: Limiter overhead at P99 must not exceed 2ms under 25k RPS.

probing_ladder.stage_1_validation: Explain how MESI cache coherence protocol handles write invalidations when 64 CPU cores attempt to update a single AtomicLong counter simultaneously.
probing_ladder.stage_2_tightening: If 100,000 requests/sec arrive and the CAS loop repeatedly fails due to high contention, what latency degradation occurs?
probing_ladder.stage_3_adversarial: How does clock drift or an NTP step adjustment affect System.nanoTime() vs System.currentTimeMillis() in rate limiting?
probing_ladder.stage_4_squeeze: We must distribute this rate limiter across 10 independent Kubernetes pods without centralized Redis to avoid network latency. How do you design local token quotas?

counter_probes.counter_question: Each Redis call over the network introduces at least 0.5ms to 1.5ms of round-trip latency. If your total request SLA is 2ms, how can you afford a network round-trip for every single check?
counter_probes.expected_staff_answer: Local in-memory token buckets with periodic asynchronous batch synchronization or token leasing from Redis should be used to avoid synchronous network overhead per request.
